title: Muriel Furrer death: Prosecutors confirm rider was not found for 85 minutes, opt against criminal proceedings
content:
The Swiss government has closed their criminal investigation into the circumstances surrounding the death of cyclist Muriel Furrer in September 2024.

Furrer, 18, had been competing in the junior world championship road race — which began in the town of Uster, near Zurich, just 10 minutes away from her childhood home in the neighbouring village of Egg.

The teenager crashed on a steep downhill descent with 45km remaining and suffered serious head injuries, dying in hospital the next day.

An investigation by The Athletic subsequently reported that Furrer lay undiscovered for around an hour-and-a-half after crashing, having disappeared from view in the heavily wooded area on leaving the road.

“I really hope that in the future, they make changes,” Furrer’s father Reto said that December. “The details are sometimes too difficult, and don’t help bring back Muriel. But we have to be sure this won’t happen again.”

However, after an 18 month investigation, the Zurich public prosecutor’s office have ruled that no third-party involvement in the crash could be established, as well as stating that “no criminally relevant breach of duty” could be found in relation to either the course’s safety or the emergency response.

They also confirmed that after Furrer crashed at 11.04am, it took 82 minutes for her to be discovered by race marshals at 12.26pm.

“Based on the police investigation, the cyclist’s fall is considered a racing accident with no evidence of criminal conduct or contributory negligence on the part of the organiser, other race participants, or third parties,” read a press release from the prosecutor’s office.

“The injured cyclist lay hidden in the undergrowth and was not visible from the road. As was customary at previous editions of this World Cycling Championship, live tracking of all athletes was not used at the event. Therefore, the sudden disappearance of an athlete was not automatically reported.”

The full investigation has not yet been released because the prosecutor’s discontinuation order has not yet become legally binding. It means that several further issues — such as whether the presence of tracking technology or extra marshalls could have shortened the delay in finding Furrer — have not yet received an answer.

“Muriel Furrer’s parents acknowledge that no criminal offence has been committed,” said a family statement provided to The Athletic. “They are particularly concerned that Muriel remained undetected for so long. It is important to them that the right lessons are learned from this incident and that similar situations are prevented in the future.”

The Athletic reported in December 2024 that two separate parties had offered local organisers and the UCI use of publicly-accessible tracking systems ahead of the race. Neither of these were taken up.

At last year’s world championships in Rwanda, where Furrer was honoured and her number retired from future women’s junior road race events, every rider had a mandatory tracker installed on their bike. The UCI confirmed earlier this month that GPS tracking in professional races will now become mandatory across a phased-in approach.

In the interim, further incidents are continuing to take place. British rider Tom Pidcock, second in Milan-Sanremo two weeks ago, crashed while descending at the Volta a Catalunya last week and wrote on Instagram: “Today I lost a life for sure. Was drinking on the descent and completely misjudged my braking. Luckily I had my radio so they could find me as no-one knew I’d crashed.”
